To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the optimal locations of central places are determined by the spatial distribution of consumer expenditures, (ii) the optimal number of central places is determined by the transportation cost function, (iii) the optimal number, location and size of central places depend on the spatial distribution of expenditures and the transportation cost function.

(1) there is a unique equilibrium number of central places on a linear market, (2) this equilibrium is a function of expenditure shares in consumption by commodity, (3) the equilibrium number is independent of the transportation cost functions used, (4) the number of central places is an inverse function of the storage cost by commodity, and (5) the equilibrium number of centralplaces is an inverse function to the capital cost of retailers.

the equilibrium locations of retailers are determined by the relative magnitudes of transportation costs, storage costs, and the cost of capital, and that the equilibrium location of a retailer depends on the relative magnitudes (in the aggregate) of the transportation and storage costs of all commodities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a model for the location of retail central places in a linear market.
the following questions: (1) What are the equilibrium spatial configurations of retail central places?
the following questions: (1) How do households allocate their expenditures among the various types of retail outlets?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the theory of central places presented here is the first model to incorporate all of the major economic forces that determine the location of retail central places.
the theory is a useful extension of existing theories of central places and provides an alternative approach to the problem.

the Contextual Theory has been successful in providing a framework within which the economic theory can be modified to account for a number of phenomena that are important to the understanding of the location of retailing activities in a spatial context.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a model of retail central places that can be used to predict the locations of central places on a linear market and to explain the spatial distribution of retailing activity.
the Contextual Theory has the potential to become the basis for a new theory of retailing central places.
the model provides a theoretical framework that can be used to explain the spatial distribution of central places and the spatial patterns of retail sales.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spatial relationship between households and retailing central places is determined by the parameters of the model.
the spatial distribution of retail central places is not determined by the spatial distribution of households.
the equilibrium locations of retailers are determined jointly by the locations of households, the transportation cost functions, the storage costs of commodities, and the costs of capital.
